questions.question: What is @RestController in Spring Boot?
questions.title: @RestController annotation explained
questions.direct_answer: **@RestController** is a meta-annotation combining **@Controller** and **@ResponseBody**. It marks a class as a web controller and automatically serializes each method's return value to JSON (via **Jackson**) in the HTTP response body — so you don't add `@ResponseBody` to every method. It's the standard annotation for REST APIs that return data rather than HTML views.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody and where the controller sits in the request flow (DispatcherServlet → controller → service → repository).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying it 'just makes controllers' without mentioning automatic response-body serialization, or using plain @Controller for a REST API and getting view-resolution 404s.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Jackson is the default serializer, that @RestController only affects responses (you still need @RequestBody for input), and trace the request through the DispatcherServlet.

sections.title: What @RestController Does in Spring Boot
sections.content:
**@RestController** is a **meta-annotation** combining **@Controller** (marks a class as a Spring MVC controller) and **@ResponseBody** (serialize the return value straight into the HTTP response body). Without it, you'd repeat `@ResponseBody` on every REST method.

The key insight: REST APIs return **data** (usually JSON), not **views** (HTML). With `@RestController`, Spring Boot converts your Java objects to JSON using **Jackson** automatically — you return a Java object and Spring handles serialization. The controller is the entry point that the **DispatcherServlet** routes a request to; from there your controller typically calls a `@Service`, which calls a `@Repository`, which hits the database.

sections.title: Where the Controller Sits in the Request Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A["Client
(browser / app)"] --> B["DispatcherServlet
front controller"] B --> C["@RestController
route + deserialize"] C --> D["@Service
business logic"] D --> E["@Repository
data access"] E --> F[("Database")] C -. "Java object -> JSON" .-> A ```

sections.title: @Controller without @ResponseBody — view resolution, 404
@RestController — JSON serialized automatically
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Controller and forgetting @ResponseBody**: Spring tries to resolve a view name from your return value, causing 404s. Use `@RestController` for APIs.
- **Returning a plain String and expecting raw text**: Jackson wraps it in quotes as JSON. For raw text set `produces = MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE`.
- **Thinking @RestController handles input**: it only affects responses. Reading incoming JSON still needs `@RequestBody`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody** — one convenience annotation.
- **Automatic JSON** — return values serialized by Jackson, no manual code.
- **No view resolution** — unlike `@Controller`, it never looks for HTML templates.
- **Class-level** — applies `@ResponseBody` to every method.
- **Responses only** — use `@RequestBody` for input; `ResponseEntity` for custom status/headers.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The RestController annotation is a Spring Boot annotation that makes building REST APIs much simpler. It combines two annotations: Controller, which marks the class as a web controller, and ResponseBody, which tells Spring to write the return value directly into the HTTP response body. The big benefit is that every method in the class automatically sends JSON back to the client without you manually converting objects or adding ResponseBody everywhere.

For example, if I have a method that returns an Order object, Spring Boot uses Jackson, the default JSON library, to serialize it to JSON, matching the field names in your Java class to JSON properties. This is perfect for REST APIs because you are returning data, not HTML views.

It helps to know where the controller sits in the request flow. A request from the client first hits the dispatcher servlet, which is the front controller. The dispatcher servlet routes it to the right RestController method. The controller usually calls a service for the business logic, the service calls a repository for data access, and the repository talks to the database. On the way back, the controller's return value is converted to JSON and sent to the client.

One thing freshers get wrong is using plain Controller when they mean to build a REST API. With plain Controller, Spring tries to find an HTML template and you get 404 errors. Another point: RestController only affects responses. To read incoming JSON in a POST or PUT, you still need the RequestBody annotation. So for an API consumed by a frontend or mobile app, RestController is exactly what you want.

speakable_v2.hook: @RestController is just two annotations merged into one — and knowing which two tells you exactly what it does.

beats.text: @RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody into one class-level annotation. @Controller tells Spring MVC this class handles HTTP requests. @ResponseBody tells Spring to serialize the return value directly to the HTTP response as JSON — don't look for a view template.

Before @RestController existed, you had to add @ResponseBody to every single method in a REST controller. @RestController applies it at the class level so you write it once. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, Jackson is already on the classpath via starter-web, so it handles the Java-to-JSON conversion automatically. You just return objects.

Walk me through how a request flows from the client to the database and back.

questions.question: What is the difference between @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping?
questions.title: HTTP method mapping annotations in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: They map a method to a specific HTTP verb: **@GetMapping** for reads (safe, idempotent), **@PostMapping** for creating (not idempotent), **@PutMapping** for full replacement (idempotent), **@DeleteMapping** for removal (idempotent). All four are shorthand for `@RequestMapping(method = ...)` and enforce RESTful semantics that affect caching and retries.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands HTTP verb semantics (safe/idempotent) and maps them to the right Spring annotations and CRUD operations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to @PostMapping for everything, which breaks caching, history, and idempotency expectations.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain idempotency precisely — GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent, POST is not — and how that guides retries and API design.

sections.title: Understanding HTTP Mapping Annotations
sections.content:
These four annotations are **shorthand** for `@RequestMapping` with a fixed **HTTP verb**. Before Spring 4.3 you wrote `@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)` — verbose and error-prone.

They aren't just sugar; they enforce **RESTful semantics**. **@GetMapping** *retrieves* data (safe and idempotent — no state change, same result every call). **@PostMapping** *creates* (not idempotent — two calls create two resources). **@PutMapping** *replaces* an entire resource (idempotent). **@DeleteMapping** *removes* (idempotent). These distinctions guide clients, proxies, and caches — a browser caches GET but not POST, and a client can safely retry an idempotent PUT after a timeout.

sections.title: Verbs, Semantics, Operations
sections.content:
amber|@GetMapping|~Read|safe + idempotent|cacheable|fetch one or many
blue|@PostMapping|~Create|NOT idempotent|server assigns id|returns 201
emerald|@PutMapping|~Replace|idempotent|client knows the URL|full update
violet|@DeleteMapping|~Remove|idempotent|safe to retry|often returns 204

sections.title: The Four Verbs
sections.content:
| Annotation | Verb | Operation | Idempotent? | Typical status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `@GetMapping` | GET | Read | Yes (safe) | 200 |
| `@PostMapping` | POST | Create | No | 201 Created |
| `@PutMapping` | PUT | Replace | Yes | 200 / 204 |
| `@DeleteMapping` | DELETE | Remove | Yes | 204 No Content |
| `@PatchMapping` | PATCH | Partial update | Not required | 200 |

sections.title: Anti-pattern — POST for everything
RESTful — the right verb per operation
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **POST for everything**: works, but breaks caching, browser history, and idempotency, and confuses API consumers.
- **Ignoring idempotency**: PUT/DELETE called twice should be safe; don't throw if the resource already exists/was deleted.
- **Confusing PUT and POST**: POST creates at an unknown URL (server assigns id); PUT replaces at a known URL (client provides id).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **GET** — safe and idempotent; read only, cacheable.
- **POST** — not idempotent; creates a new resource (201 + `Location`).
- **PUT** — idempotent; full replacement at a known URL.
- **DELETE** — idempotent; removal, usually 204.
- **Shorthand** — each replaces `@RequestMapping(method = ...)` and combines with the class-level base path.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
These four annotations map different HTTP methods to controller methods, and each has a specific purpose in REST APIs. GetMapping is for reading data. It is safe and idempotent, meaning it does not change anything on the server and calling it multiple times gives the same result, so responses can be cached. You use it to fetch a list of users or a single product by ID. PostMapping is for creating new resources. It is not idempotent, so calling it twice creates two separate resources. You use it when submitting a form or placing an order where the server generates the ID, and it typically returns 201 Created.

PutMapping is for replacing an entire resource at a known URL. It is idempotent, so updating the same product ten times with the same data leaves you with the same end state. DeleteMapping is for removing resources, and it is also idempotent, so deleting something already gone should just succeed or return a 404.

A common mistake freshers make is using POST for everything because it works. But that breaks REST conventions and prevents browsers and proxies from caching responses, and it removes the safety of retrying idempotent calls. Another mistake is not understanding idempotency and writing PUT logic that fails if you call it twice. The key is matching the HTTP verb to the operation's semantics, which makes your API predictable and lets clients, caches, and tools behave correctly.

speakable_v2.hook: Each HTTP verb has its own mapping annotation — and each maps to a specific CRUD operation in REST design.

beats.text: All four are shortcuts for @RequestMapping with a specific HTTP method pre-set. They exist purely for readability. Here's the standard REST mapping used in a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application.

rows: Read — fetch a resource or list
Replace — update an existing resource fully

beats.text: Always use the specific annotation — @GetMapping is far clearer than @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET). They communicate intent in one glance.

followup_questions: What does idempotent mean, and which verbs are idempotent?
What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
What HTTP status code should a successful POST return?

seo.meta_description: Understand Spring Boot's HTTP method mapping annotations — @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping.

questions.question: What is the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?
questions.title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: **@PathVariable** extracts a value from the URL path itself (e.g. `/users/123` → `123`), identifying *which* resource. **@RequestParam** extracts a value from the query string (e.g. `/users?status=active` → `active`), used to filter/sort/paginate *how* you retrieve it. Path variables are usually required; request params are often optional.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands URL structure — path segments vs query parameters — and the RESTful semantics of each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @RequestParam for resource IDs (e.g. /users?id=123), or forgetting @RequestParam is required by default.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State that path variables are part of resource identity while query params are optional modifiers, and show required=false / defaultValue handling.

sections.title: Path Variables vs Query Parameters
sections.content:
In `GET /api/users/42?status=active&sort=name`, the `42` is a **path segment** identifying which user; `status` and `sort` are **query parameters** that filter or modify retrieval.

**@PathVariable** reads from the path template you define (`/users/{userId}`) — usually **required**, representing core resource identity. **@RequestParam** reads from the query string (after `?`) — typically **optional** filters, pagination, or sorting. The RESTful principle: path variables define *what* resource you address; query params define *how* you retrieve or filter it.

sections.title: Which One When
sections.content:
amber|@PathVariable|~From the path|/users/{id}|required by default|resource identity
blue|@RequestParam|~From the query string|/users?status=active|often optional|filter / sort / page
emerald|REST convention|~What vs how|path = which resource|query = how to shape it|keep it consistent
violet|Optional handling|~Defaults|required = false|defaultValue = "..."|else 400 if missing

sections.title: PathVariable vs RequestParam
sections.content:
| Aspect | @PathVariable | @RequestParam |
|---|---|---|
| URL location | Part of the path | After `?` in query string |
| Purpose | Identify which resource | Filter, sort, paginate |
| Required by default | Yes (path must match) | Yes — set `required=false` to relax |
| REST role | Core resource identifier | Optional modifiers |
| Example | `/users/{id}` | `/users?status=active` |

sections.title: Wrong — ID as a query param, fragile optionals
Right — ID in the path, optional query params
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Query param for resource IDs**: `/users?id=123` breaks REST — the ID is identity, not a filter. Use `/users/123`.
- **Optional params not handled**: `@RequestParam` is required by default; omit the value and Spring returns 400. Use `required = false` or `defaultValue`.
- **Mixing conventions**: don't expose both `/users/{id}` and `/users?id=123` — pick one and stay consistent.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@PathVariable** — reads `{...}` placeholders from the path; usually required.
- **@RequestParam** — reads values after `?`; often optional.
- **REST role** — path = which resource, query = how to filter/shape it.
- **Optional handling** — `required=false` or `defaultValue` for query params.
- **Naming** — `@PathVariable("userId")` when the method param name differs from the template.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
PathVariable and RequestParam both extract data from the URL, but they read from different places and serve different purposes. PathVariable pulls values from the path itself, the part before any question mark. For example, in slash users slash 123, the 123 is a path variable. You define the endpoint as GetMapping slash users slash open brace id close brace and use PathVariable Long id to capture it. Path variables identify which resource you are working with, so they are usually required and represent things like IDs or keys.

RequestParam pulls values from the query string, the part after the question mark. In slash users question mark status equals active, status is a query parameter. You use RequestParam String status to read it. Query params are typically optional filters, pagination controls, or sorting options.

The RESTful convention is that path variables define the resource identity, while query params modify how you retrieve it. A common mistake is using a query param for a resource ID, like slash users question mark id equals 123, which breaks REST. Another mistake is not handling optional params, because by default RequestParam is required, so if the client omits it Spring throws a 400. You fix that with required equals false or a default value. The simple rule: path variables are structural and required, query params are flexible modifiers.

speakable_v2.hook: Both extract values from the URL — but from different parts. Path variable is which resource, query param is how to filter it.

beats.text: The difference is where in the URL the value comes from.

Mental model that works: path variable answers 'which resource?' — GET /users/42 fetches user 42. Query parameter answers 'how should the response be shaped?' — GET /users?status=active&page=1 filters and paginates the list. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, you'll use both in the same controller all the time.

followup_questions: How do you make a @RequestParam optional or give it a default?
Why is using a query parameter for a resource ID considered non-RESTful?
What is @RequestBody and how does it differ from these two?

seo.meta_description: Understand the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam in Spring Boot REST controllers.

questions.question: What is @RequestBody and how does it work?
questions.title: @RequestBody in Spring Boot REST controllers
questions.direct_answer: **@RequestBody** tells Spring to read the HTTP request body and **deserialize** it into a Java object using **Jackson** (matching JSON keys to fields). It's used with POST/PUT/PATCH to receive JSON payloads. It's the input counterpart to `@ResponseBody`, and you typically pair it with **@Valid** to validate the deserialized object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands automatic request-payload deserialization in Spring REST APIs and that it doesn't validate by itself.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you must read the InputStream and parse JSON manually, or deserializing without adding @Valid so invalid data reaches business logic.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Jackson field-name matching (@JsonProperty for mismatches) and pairing @RequestBody with @Valid for format + constraint safety.

sections.title: How @RequestBody Deserializes HTTP Payloads
sections.content:
**@RequestBody** is the **input counterpart** to `@ResponseBody`. While `@ResponseBody` (built into `@RestController`) serializes Java to JSON for responses, `@RequestBody` deserializes JSON from the request body into Java objects. When a client POSTs a JSON payload, Spring needs to convert that JSON string into a Java object your method can use.

`@RequestBody` says: "read the body, parse it as JSON, map it to this parameter." **Jackson** does the work, matching JSON keys to Java field names — `"email"` maps to an `email` field. You write no parsing code; your method receives a fully populated object ready for validation and business logic.

sections.title: Request Body, Step by Step
sections.content:
amber|@RequestBody|~Reads the body|on POST/PUT/PATCH|one per method|input side of REST
blue|Jackson maps it|~JSON -> object|keys match field names|@JsonProperty for mismatches|case-sensitive
emerald|@Valid pairs with it|~Enforce rules|@NotBlank, @Email|fails -> 400|runs after parsing
violet|Content-Type|~Tells Spring the format|application/json|else 415|set by the client

sections.title: Manual parsing — verbose and unnecessary
@RequestBody + @Valid — automatic and validated
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Manual parsing**: you don't read the InputStream or call ObjectMapper yourself — declare the parameter type and Spring deserializes it.
- **Field name mismatches**: JSON `user_name` won't map to `userName` without `@JsonProperty("user_name")`.
- **No validation**: `@RequestBody` parses but doesn't validate — add `@Valid` and constraints.
- **Using it with GET**: GET shouldn't have a body; many clients/proxies strip it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Automatic deserialization** — Jackson converts request JSON into a Java object.
- **Field matching** — JSON keys map to field names (case-sensitive); use `@JsonProperty` for mismatches.
- **POST/PUT/PATCH** — used with methods that accept payloads, not GET.
- **Pair with @Valid** — format safety from `@RequestBody`, constraint checks from `@Valid`.
- **Content-Type** — client should send `application/json`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
RequestBody tells Spring to read the HTTP request body and convert it into a Java object. It is used mainly with POST, PUT, and PATCH requests where the client sends data in the body, usually as JSON. For example, when creating a new customer, the client sends a JSON payload with name and email. You annotate the method parameter with RequestBody, and Spring automatically deserializes that JSON into a Java object. The default library doing this work is Jackson, which matches JSON keys to Java field names. If the JSON has an email property, Jackson looks for an email field in your class.

The big advantage is you do not write any parsing code. You just declare the parameter type and Spring handles the conversion. One thing freshers often miss is validation. RequestBody deserializes the data, but it does not validate it. You add Valid before RequestBody and use annotations like NotBlank or Email on the fields to enforce rules. If the JSON field names do not match your Java fields, like user underscore name versus userName, you add a JsonProperty annotation to map them.

Another mistake is expecting it to work with GET requests. GET should not have a body by HTTP convention, and many tools strip it. So RequestBody is really for data submission in POST and PUT. The bottom line is it is the input side of REST APIs, converting incoming JSON into Java objects you can work with, and pairing it with Valid gives you both format safety and business-rule validation in one place.

speakable_v2.hook: @RequestBody is the bridge between the JSON in the request body and your Java object — Jackson handles the conversion.

beats.text: When a client POSTs a JSON body, Spring needs to turn that JSON string into a Java object. @RequestBody triggers that. Jackson reads the JSON field names and maps them to matching Java fields on your DTO. If the client sends name and email, Jackson creates a CreateUserRequest with those fields populated — no manual parsing needed.

The power move is combining @RequestBody with @Valid. @RequestBody handles format parsing — if the JSON is malformed, it fails with a 400. @Valid then validates the constraints declared on the DTO fields (@NotBlank, @Email). In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, using both annotations on a @PostMapping parameter gives you format safety and business rule validation in one line.

followup_questions: Why doesn't @RequestBody validate the object on its own?
How do you map a snake_case JSON key to a camelCase Java field?
What happens if the request Content-Type isn't application/json?

seo.meta_description: Understand @RequestBody in Spring Boot — how Jackson deserializes the HTTP request body into a Java object.

questions.question: How do you return different HTTP status codes in Spring Boot?
questions.title: HTTP status codes in Spring Boot — ResponseEntity and @ResponseStatus
questions.direct_answer: Two main ways: **@ResponseStatus** on a method or exception class sets a *fixed* status code, while returning **ResponseEntity<T>** lets you set the status, headers, and body *dynamically* at runtime. Use `@ResponseStatus` for predictable cases (e.g. 204 on delete); use `ResponseEntity` when the status depends on logic (200 vs 404, 201 + Location).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can signal proper status codes beyond 200 and knows when to use @ResponseStatus vs ResponseEntity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning 200 for everything (including creation and deletion), or not knowing ResponseEntity controls status, headers, and body.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the common codes (201 Created + Location, 204 No Content, 404), and show Optional.map(ResponseEntity::ok).orElse(notFound).

sections.title: Two Approaches to HTTP Status Control
sections.content:
Spring Boot gives two ways to control status codes. **@ResponseStatus** is *declarative* — annotate a method or custom exception with a fixed code; great when the status never changes. **ResponseEntity<T>** is *programmatic* — you decide status, headers, and body at runtime based on logic.

Think of `@ResponseStatus` as a fixed sign and `ResponseEntity` as a changeable display. Production APIs use both: `@ResponseStatus` for predictable error cases (and exception handlers), `ResponseEntity` when the response varies with data.

sections.title: Status Control + Common Codes
sections.content:
amber|@ResponseStatus|~Fixed code|on method or exception|simple, no body control|e.g. 204 on delete
blue|ResponseEntity|~Dynamic code|status + headers + body|builder pattern|conditional 200/404
emerald|Common codes|~Use the right one|201 Created (+Location)|204 No Content|404 Not Found
violet|Pitfall|~Not everything is 200|create -> 201|delete -> 204|missing -> 404

sections.title: @ResponseStatus vs ResponseEntity
sections.content:
| Aspect | @ResponseStatus | ResponseEntity<T> |
|---|---|---|
| Status code | Fixed at compile time | Dynamic at runtime |
| Flexibility | Single status only | Full control: status, headers, body |
| Use case | Fixed responses, exceptions | Conditional / variable responses |
| Return type | Any type or `void` | Must return `ResponseEntity<T>` |
| Custom headers | No | Yes (e.g. `Location`) |

sections.title: Anti-pattern — 200 OK for everything
Correct — meaningful status codes
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Always 200 OK**: creation should be 201, deletion 204, missing 404 — otherwise clients can't tell what happened.
- **ResponseEntity body confusion**: with no body, call `.build()` (e.g. `notFound().build()`).
- **No Location header on 201**: clients shouldn't have to guess the new resource's URL; include `Location`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@ResponseStatus** — fixed code on a method or exception class.
- **ResponseEntity<T>** — runtime control of status, headers, and body via a builder.
- **Common codes** — 200 OK, 201 Created (+ `Location`), 204 No Content, 404 Not Found.
- **Optional pattern** — `find(id).map(ResponseEntity::ok).orElse(notFound().build())`.
- **Mix both** — `ResponseEntity` for variable responses, `@ResponseStatus` for exceptions/fixed cases.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
There are two main ways to return different status codes in Spring Boot. The simpler one is the ResponseStatus annotation. You put it on a method or an exception class with a fixed status code like NO_CONTENT or CREATED. This works great when the status never changes, like a DELETE method that always returns 204.

The more flexible approach is returning ResponseEntity from your controller method. ResponseEntity gives you full control at runtime. You can set the status code, add custom headers, and include a body all in one object. For example, if you are creating a new order, you return ResponseEntity dot status CREATED with a Location header pointing to the new resource, which is 201. If you are fetching something that might not exist, you can return dot ok if it is found, or dot notFound dot build if it is missing, which is 404.

The key difference is that ResponseStatus is fixed at compile time, while ResponseEntity lets you decide the status based on your logic. A common mistake freshers make is always returning 200 OK for everything. You should use 201 for creation, 204 for deletion, and 404 when something is not found. A neat pattern is taking an Optional from the service, mapping it to ResponseEntity dot ok if present, and falling back to notFound dot build if empty, which gives you 200 or 404 in a single line. In production you will use ResponseEntity most of the time because responses depend on data, and ResponseStatus for exceptions and simple fixed cases.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring defaults to 200 OK. To return 201, 204, or a dynamic 404, you need to take control of the status code.

beats.text: Two ways to control the HTTP status code in a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application. For a fixed status that's always the same, add @ResponseStatus on the method — @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) makes a POST return 201 every time, @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT) makes a DELETE return 204.

For dynamic status codes that depend on the result, use ResponseEntity as the return type. ResponseEntity.ok(user) returns 200 with the user body. ResponseEntity.notFound().build() returns 404 with no body. You can chain these with Optional.map() to return 200 if the record exists and 404 if it doesn't — in a single line. ResponseEntity also lets you set custom response headers when needed.

followup_questions: What is the difference between 200 OK and 201 Created?
How do you return a 404 only when a record is missing?
How do you set a custom response header with ResponseEntity?

questions.question: What is @RequestMapping at the class level used for?
questions.title: @RequestMapping class-level base path
questions.direct_answer: **@RequestMapping** at the class level sets a **base path prefix** for every method in the controller. With `@RequestMapping("/api/users")` on the class and `@GetMapping("/{id}")` on a method, the full URL is `/api/users/{id}` — the paths **compose**, they don't override. It keeps controllers DRY and is the standard place for API versioning like `/api/v1`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands URL composition from class-level and method-level mappings and the DRY benefit.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the class path overrides the method path, or repeating the base path on every method annotation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that class-level mapping can also set produces/consumes/headers, and that versioning (/api/v1 → /api/v2) lives here.

sections.title: Class-Level Request Mapping for Path Prefixes
sections.content:
**@RequestMapping** at the class level defines a **base URL prefix** applied to every method in that controller. Spring **concatenates** the class path with each method path — they compose, not override. With `@RequestMapping("/api/products")` on the class and `@GetMapping("/{id}")` on a method, the full URL is `/api/products/{id}`.

This follows **DRY** — declare the common path once instead of before every method — and groups related endpoints logically. Class-level mapping can also set shared attributes like **produces**, **consumes**, and **headers** for all methods, and it's where you put API version prefixes such as `/api/v1`.

sections.title: How Paths Compose
sections.content:
amber|Class-level path|~Base prefix|@RequestMapping("/api/users")|applies to all methods|declared once
blue|Method-level path|~Relative part|@GetMapping("/{id}")|appended to base|full = /api/users/{id}
emerald|Shared attributes|~Set once|produces = JSON|consumes, headers|apply to all methods
violet|Versioning|~Lives here|/api/v1/users|bump to /api/v2|separate versions cleanly

sections.title: Repeating the base path on every method
Class-level base path — DRY and versionable
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking it overrides**: the class path doesn't replace the method path — they combine. `@GetMapping("/list")` becomes `/api/resource/list`.
- **Repeating the base path**: writing the full path on every method violates DRY and makes renames painful.
- **Missing the leading slash**: use `/api/users`, not `api/users`, to avoid context-path routing surprises.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Composition** — class + method paths concatenate into the final URL.
- **DRY** — declare the common prefix once.
- **Grouping** — all endpoints for a resource live under one prefix.
- **Versioning** — `/api/v1` vs `/api/v2` at the class level.
- **Shared attributes** — `produces`/`consumes`/`headers` can be set class-wide.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
RequestMapping at the class level sets a base URL path prefix that applies to every method in that controller. Spring Boot combines the class-level path with each method-level path to build the final endpoint URL. They do not override each other, they stack together. For example, if you put RequestMapping slash api slash orders at the class level and a method has GetMapping with slash open brace id, the complete URL becomes slash api slash orders slash id.

This is really useful because it follows the DRY principle. You declare the common part once instead of typing slash api slash orders before every method. It also keeps your code organized by grouping all endpoints for one resource under the same prefix. You will see this in every production REST API because it makes the code cleaner and easier to refactor. If you need to change the base path, you only update it in one place.

One thing freshers miss is that you can also set other attributes at the class level, like produces equals application slash json so all methods return JSON, and it is the natural place to handle API versioning, like slash api slash v1 slash customers, bumping to v2 when you need a new version. A common mistake is thinking the class annotation overrides the method annotation, when it actually combines with it. Another is repeating the base path in every method because they did not know about class-level mapping.

speakable_v2.hook: Class-level @RequestMapping sets a base path so you don't repeat /users on every single method.

beats.text: @RequestMapping on the class sets a root path that all method-level mappings are relative to. Add @RequestMapping('/users') to the class, then @GetMapping('/{id}') on a method, and the full URL becomes GET /users/{id}. Without the class-level mapping, you'd have to write /users/{id} on every method annotation — repetitive and error-prone.

The standard pattern in a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application: one controller class per resource, with the resource base path on the class. UserController has @RequestMapping('/api/v1/users'). OrderController has @RequestMapping('/api/v1/orders'). Methods then only declare the relative path — /{id}, /search, whatever they handle. URL versioning also happens here — bump the class-level path to /api/v2/users when you need to version an endpoint.

questions.question: What is @ControllerAdvice and how do you handle exceptions globally in Spring Boot?
questions.title: @ControllerAdvice for global exception handling
questions.direct_answer: **@ControllerAdvice** (or **@RestControllerAdvice**) centralizes exception handling for all controllers in one class. Combined with **@ExceptionHandler** methods, it catches specific exceptions and returns consistent error responses — removing try-catch from every controller method. It uses Spring's interception so a `ResourceNotFoundException` becomes a 404, validation failures become 400, etc., in one place.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows how to centralize error handling instead of repeating try-catch, and produce consistent structured error responses.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping every controller method in try-catch, or returning raw exception messages that leak internal details.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @RestControllerAdvice (adds @ResponseBody), structured error bodies (timestamp/message/status), and RFC 9457 ProblemDetail support in Spring 6.

sections.title: Centralized Exception Handling with @ControllerAdvice
sections.content:
**@ControllerAdvice** handles exceptions globally across all controllers. Without it you'd duplicate try-catch in every method. Instead, you write one class that intercepts exceptions thrown anywhere and converts them into proper HTTP error responses, using **@ExceptionHandler** methods — each catching a specific exception type.

It applies a cross-cutting concern (error handling) in one place, giving **consistent error responses** (same JSON shape, same status codes) and DRY code. In Spring Boot 3.2 prefer **@RestControllerAdvice** (it adds `@ResponseBody` so your error objects serialize to JSON), and consider the standard `ProblemDetail` (RFC 9457) body format.

sections.title: Global Error Handling
sections.content:
amber|@RestControllerAdvice|~One class, all controllers|@ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody|intercepts thrown exceptions|JSON error bodies
blue|@ExceptionHandler|~Per exception type|maps to a status|ResourceNotFound -> 404|MethodArgumentNotValid -> 400
emerald|Structured response|~Consistent shape|timestamp, status|message, path|or ProblemDetail (RFC 9457)
rose|Pitfalls|~Stay safe|don't leak stack traces|sanitize messages|handle the catch-all 500

sections.title: try-catch in every controller — duplicated everywhere
One @RestControllerAdvice — consistent, centralized
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **try-catch in every controller**: duplicates error logic and produces inconsistent responses. Centralize with `@RestControllerAdvice`.
- **Leaking raw messages**: `ex.getMessage()` can expose table names or paths. Return sanitized, structured errors.
- **No catch-all**: handling only custom exceptions leaves the default white-label page for the rest — add an `Exception.class` handler.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@ControllerAdvice / @RestControllerAdvice** — one global handler for all controllers (the latter adds `@ResponseBody`).
- **@ExceptionHandler** — maps a specific exception type to a response.
- **Consistent errors** — return a structured body (status, message, timestamp) or `ProblemDetail`.
- **Catch-all** — add an `Exception.class` handler for unexpected errors (500).
- **Don't leak** — sanitize messages; never expose stack traces to clients.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
ControllerAdvice is a Spring annotation that lets you handle exceptions globally across your entire application in one centralized class. Without it, you would need try-catch blocks in every controller method, duplicating the same error handling everywhere. Instead, you create a class annotated with ControllerAdvice, or better, RestControllerAdvice, and you write methods annotated with ExceptionHandler. Each method catches a specific exception type, like ResourceNotFoundException or a validation exception. When any controller throws that exception, Spring routes it to your handler method, where you return a custom error response with the right HTTP status code and a clean JSON structure.

For example, if a user requests an order that does not exist, the controller throws ResourceNotFoundException, your handler catches it, and you return a 404 with a message like order not found. Validation failures from the request body throw MethodArgumentNotValidException, which you map to a 400 with the field errors. You should also have a catch-all handler for the generic Exception so unexpected errors return a clean 500 instead of the default white-label error page.

One thing freshers miss is returning structured error objects with fields like status, message, and timestamp, rather than raw exception messages that might leak internal details like table names. In Spring Boot 3, you can also use the standard ProblemDetail format defined by RFC 9457. In production, every REST API should have a global exception handler because it ensures consistent, professional error responses and keeps your controllers focused on business logic.

speakable_v2.hook: Without @ControllerAdvice, every controller method needs its own try-catch. With it, you handle all exceptions in one place.

beats.text: @ControllerAdvice is a class-level annotation that makes a class an interceptor for exceptions thrown by any controller in the application. You add @ExceptionHandler methods inside it — each one handles a specific exception type. When UserController throws a ResourceNotFoundException, your advice class catches it, runs your handler method, and returns the structured error response you define.

In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, use @RestControllerAdvice instead — it combines @ControllerAdvice and @ResponseBody so your error response objects serialize to JSON automatically. One class handles all your exception-to-HTTP-response mappings: ResourceNotFoundException becomes 404, MethodArgumentNotValidException becomes 400, any unhandled RuntimeException becomes 500. Consistent error format across the entire API.
